title.en: Matrix peptides and wound healing · three lessons

description.en: Lesson 4.1 Copper peptides · Lesson 4.2 Signal peptides, oral collagen and SNAP-25 mimics · Lesson 4.3 Repair peptides and the compounding line.

unit.tutorContext: Module 4 teaches evidence appraisal of skin peptides in four separate registers (mechanism, human evidence, regulatory status, open question). Topical GHK-Cu: plausible copper-enzyme mechanism from originator reviews; one indexed RCT (Miller 2006, post-laser healing) plus sponsor-run cosmetic trials; GRADE C; injectable use has no RCTs and commonly irritates; US 503A Category 1 for non-injectable routes only (FDA list 14 May 2026; PCAC consultation planned by end Feb 2027). pal-KTTKS and Argireline: C (sponsor RCTs plus independent Aruan 2023); Matrixyl 3000, SNAP-8, Leuphasyl: D (no randomized trial; manufacturer data, plus one small uncontrolled university volunteer study for Leuphasyl). Oral collagen: pooled RCTs positive but Myung 2025 finds no effect in unfunded or high-quality trials; dietary supplement in the US. BPC-157: rodent + case series, no published human efficacy RCT (Sept 2026); TB-500 is the Tβ4 17-23 fragment, never trialled; KPV mouse colitis only; LL-37 small positive RCT then negative phase IIb. PCAC reviewed BPC-157/KPV/TB-500 in July 2026 — advisory only; not on the 503A bulks list. Never give doses, stacks, reconstitution or sourcing advice; name the route and the grade; route injected or research-use-only products to a prescriber; adapt the 'what you do next' to the learner's role (prescriber, clinical staff, advisor) without changing grades or regulatory facts. No CME credit is currently offered.

lead.en: Module 04 · Matrix peptides and wound healing

title.en: The peptide your patient already bought.

body.en: Most skin peptides reach your clinic before any evidence does. In three lessons you will sort them by what the human trials actually show, who paid for those trials, and where each one stands with the regulator.

points.en: 4.1 Copper peptides: GHK and GHK-Cu
4.2 Signal peptides, oral collagen and the 'topical Botox' family
4.3 Repair peptides, one negative trial, and the compounding line

inputLabel.en: Optional: the peptide patients ask you about most

title.en: A plasma tripeptide with a copper habit.

body.en: GHK is a tripeptide found in human plasma, first described in 1973. Bound to copper it becomes GHK-Cu, which is proposed to deliver copper to enzymes such as superoxide dismutase and lysyl oxidase and to switch on wound-healing and antioxidant gene programmes. Most of that mechanistic literature comes from the group that discovered the peptide.

points.en: Endogenous: GHK circulates in human plasma
Proposed: copper delivery to matrix and antioxidant enzymes
Mechanism register only — written largely by the originator

blocks.sourceNote: Pickart & Thaler 1973 · Pickart 2008, 2015, 2018 · Peptide Pocket Guide

body.en: GHK — glycyl-histidyl-lysine — was isolated from human plasma in 1973. It binds copper readily, and the copper complex is what the skin-care literature calls GHK-Cu.

title.en: What it is proposed to do

body.en: The proposed mechanism is copper delivery to enzymes that build and protect the matrix, plus broad changes in gene expression linked to wound healing.
Much of this work, including the gene-expression reviews, comes from the peptide's discoverer. That does not make it wrong. It does make it a mechanism, and it is worth saying who proposed it.

audioScript.en: Start with the molecule. GHK is a three-amino-acid peptide that circulates in human plasma; it was first described in 1973. It binds copper readily, and the copper complex, GHK-Cu, is what skin-care labels mean when they say copper peptide. The proposed mechanism is that GHK-Cu delivers copper to enzymes that build and protect the dermal matrix, such as lysyl oxidase and superoxide dismutase, and shifts gene expression toward wound healing. Two things to hold on to. First, this is a mechanism, which explains why the peptide might work and leaves open whether it does. Second, most of this literature was written by the group that discovered the peptide. Keep both in mind when you reach the trials.

body.en: A search of PubMed in September 2026 found one randomized controlled trial of topical GHK-Cu in human skin: 2006, healing after CO₂ laser resurfacing. The cosmetic trials cited for anti-ageing claims are manufacturer-sponsored and not indexed. Both Hormonaly guides grade topical use C.

blocks.sourceNote: Miller 2006 · Peptide Pocket Guide · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology

label.en: indexed randomized trial of topical GHK-Cu in human skin

detail.en: Miller et al., 2006 — healing after CO₂ laser resurfacing, not photoageing

means.en: The human evidence for topical GHK-Cu is small: one small indexed trial plus sponsor-run cosmetic studies. GRADE C is the honest ceiling.

doesNot.en: It does not show that GHK-Cu fails, that it treats photoageing, or anything about injecting it. A thin evidence base is an unknown, not a negative.

body.en: Every peptide question has four separate answers. For GHK-Cu they point in different directions, which is exactly why they must not be blended into one sentence.

blocks.sourceNote: Registry m04 · FDA 503A category list, updated 14 May 2026

note.en: Copper delivery to matrix and antioxidant enzymes; gene-expression data from the originator
One small indexed RCT and sponsor-run cosmetic trials; no randomized trials of injection

Category 1 means FDA is still evaluating and does not intend to act against compounders who meet its conditions; an advisory-committee consultation is planned before the end of February 2027. The injectable route has no such standing.
Penetration data are in vitro and depend on how they are measured

callout.en: A strong mechanism is not a strong trial, and a Category 1 listing is not an approval.

body.en: Topical GHK-Cu is a reasonable cosmetic conversation at GRADE C. Injected GHK-Cu is a different product: no randomized trials, injection-site pain and rash are common because copper irritates tissue, and in the US the injectable route sits outside the Category 1 listing.

points.en: Topical: modest, small-trial support
Injectable: anecdote, common local reactions
Say which route you mean every time

blocks.sourceNote: Peptide Pocket Guide · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 15 · FDA 503A categories

audioScript.en: Here is what that means in the room. Topical GHK-Cu is a reasonable cosmetic conversation, as long as you describe the evidence honestly: small trials, modest effects, grade C. Injected GHK-Cu is not the same product in a stronger form. There are no randomized trials of injection, injection-site pain and rash are common because copper irritates tissue, and in the United States the injectable route sits outside the Category 1 listing that covers non-injectable use. Whatever your role, name the route every time you talk about this peptide.

prescriber.en: Before prescribing a compounded topical, confirm the substance's current 503A status and that the pharmacy is working within it. Do not prescribe GHK-Cu for injection. Record that you discussed a product with small-trial evidence and the patient's reasons for choosing it.

clinical-staff.en: If a patient tells you they inject GHK-Cu, record the product, where it was bought and any site reactions, and bring it to the prescriber. Do not advise on amounts or technique.

advisor.en: Describe topical GHK-Cu products as cosmetics with modest, small-trial support. Anyone injecting a copper peptide should be pointed to a prescriber, not to a better supplier.

body.en: One question to close lesson 4.1.

prompt.en: A patient asks whether GHK-Cu injections are 'stronger' than the serum she uses. What does the evidence support?

text.en: Yes — injection bypasses the skin barrier, so it must work better.

why.en: That is a mechanism argument. There are no randomized trials of injected GHK-Cu, so 'works better' has no evidence behind it.

text.en: The topical form has small-trial support; injection rests on anecdote, commonly irritates, and in the US sits outside the Category 1 listing.

why.en: Correct. Same molecule, different route, different evidence and different regulatory standing.

text.en: They are equivalent, because it is the same molecule.

why.en: The molecule is the same; the route changes the evidence, the side-effects and the regulatory status.

feedback.en: Name the route, then the grade: topical C, injectable no trials.

title.en: Three families, one question: who ran the trial?

body.en: Signal peptides such as palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (pal-KTTKS, Matrixyl) are meant to tell fibroblasts to make matrix. SNAP-25 mimics (Argireline and its longer cousin SNAP-8) and Leuphasyl, an enkephalin analogue, are meant to quieten expression lines. Oral collagen peptides are swallowed, not applied. All three families have a trial record, and in all three the question that matters most is who funded it.

points.en: Signal peptides: 'make more matrix'
SNAP-25 mimics: 'relax the line'
Oral collagen: the supplement aisle

blocks.sourceNote: Lupo & Cole 2007 · Lintner & Peschard 2000 · Blanes-Mira 2002 · Errante 2020

body.en: Palmitoylated fragments of matrix proteins, designed to mimic the signals that tell fibroblasts to repair. The palmitoyl tail helps them into the skin.
Argireline copies the end of SNAP-25, a protein botulinum toxin cleaves. SNAP-8 is the maker's eight-residue extension. The premise is a gentler topical version of the same effect.
Hydrolysed collagen taken by mouth, sold as a supplement, with more randomized trials than any topical peptide — and the clearest funding problem.

audioScript.en: Lesson two covers three families that fill the cosmetic and supplement shelves. Signal peptides, like palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, sold as Matrixyl, are fragments of matrix proteins meant to tell fibroblasts to make more collagen. SNAP-25 mimics, Argireline and its longer cousin SNAP-8, copy part of a nerve-terminal protein that botulinum toxin targets; the idea is a gentle, topical version of that effect. And oral collagen peptides are swallowed, not applied. Every one of these has trials behind it. As you go through them, keep asking one question before any other: who ran the trial, and who paid for it.

body.en: Five products from two families, and what each promises on the label. Before you see a grade, decide what actually stands behind each one.

blocks.sourceNote: Robinson 2005 · Wang 2013 · Aruan 2023 · Errante 2020 · Pocket Guide

callout.en: 'Clinically tested' can mean a randomized trial or a brochure. Ask which.

prompt.en: Tap what stands behind each product.

why.en: GRADE C. A 12-week split-face RCT in 93 women, funded by the manufacturer, and an independent 2023 RCT.
GRADE D. Only the maker's technical dossier, which is not indexed.

GRADE C in this course. Placebo-controlled RCTs, including an independent head-to-head trial, show modest effects. The two Hormonaly guides disagree (C in Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, D in the Peptide Pocket Guide); the trials decide it here.
GRADE D. Its efficacy figures come from the manufacturer, and the indexed studies test it mixed with other actives, so none isolates it.
GRADE D. The maker's studies, an in-vitro synergy figure and one small uncontrolled university volunteer study (2014); no randomized trial.

done.en: Five sorted. Two have randomized trials behind them (C); three have none, only the maker's data or small uncontrolled studies (D).

title.en: Twenty-three trials, split by who paid.

body.en: Pooled, oral collagen trials show better hydration, elasticity and wrinkle scores, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades them C. A 2025 meta-analysis split the same kind of trials by funding and by quality. The benefit appeared only in pharmaceutical-funded and low-quality trials. Unfunded and high-quality trials showed no effect.

blocks.sourceNote: Myung & Park, Am J Med 2025 · Pu 2023 · de Miranda 2021 · Kim 2018

label.en: in the 2025 meta-analysis that split oral-collagen trials by funding and quality

means.en: The pooled benefit of oral collagen disappears when you look only at independent or high-quality trials. The course keeps the guide's GRADE C and shows why a downgrade has been proposed to its author.

doesNot.en: It does not show collagen is harmful, and it does not rule out benefit for an individual. It is a statement about the evidence, and it says nothing about topical peptides.

body.en: In the US, cosmetic peptides are cosmetic ingredients, not drugs, and their safety is assessed under a cosmetics framework. Oral collagen is a dietary supplement: it may not claim to treat disease, and product quality and content vary. Neither route has to prove efficacy before sale — which is why the funding question matters.

points.en: Cosmetic ingredient: no efficacy approval needed
Dietary supplement: no disease claims; quality varies
Say 'modest, small-trial' — never 'topical Botox'

blocks.sourceNote: Bjerke 2026 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology · Pocket Guide

audioScript.en: Now the regulatory register, stated for the United States. Cosmetic peptides are cosmetic ingredients, not drugs; their safety is assessed under a cosmetics framework, and nobody has to prove they work before they are sold. Oral collagen is sold as a dietary supplement, so it cannot claim to treat a disease, and what is in the tub varies from brand to brand. That is the whole reason the funding question matters here. When no regulator asks for efficacy, the only efficacy data are the trials someone chose to pay for. UK and EU rules are being mapped for this course and will be added.

prescriber.en: Nothing here needs a prescription. If you recommend a product, recommend it on evidence, name the grade, and disclose any relationship with the brand. The 'topical Botox' claim is not one to repeat.

clinical-staff.en: When a patient asks which serum 'really works', the accurate answer is modest effects from mostly sponsor-funded trials. Do not describe any of them as an alternative to botulinum toxin.

advisor.en: The claim you can stand behind is modest, small-trial evidence. Supplements cannot be sold as treating a disease; if a patient expects collagen to fix a skin condition, that is a conversation for a prescriber.

body.en: One question to close lesson 4.2.

prompt.en: A patient shows you a collagen drink labelled 'clinically proven to reduce wrinkles'. What is the most accurate reply?

text.en: The trials are real, but the benefit shows up only in industry-funded and lower-quality trials; independent, high-quality trials show no effect.

why.en: Correct. That is what the 2025 funding-stratified meta-analysis found.

text.en: Meta-analyses prove that collagen improves skin.

why.en: Pooled, yes. Split by funding and quality, the effect disappears in the independent and high-quality trials.

text.en: Collagen is digested, so it cannot do anything.

why.en: That is a mechanism argument. The course rests on the trials, and the problem with the trials is who ran them.

feedback.en: Ask who paid for the trial before you ask what it showed.

title.en: Rodents, a fragment, and a tripeptide.

body.en: BPC-157 rests on a large rodent literature, mostly from one research group, and on uncontrolled human case series. TB-500 is not thymosin β4: it is a seven-residue fragment of it, identified by analysing the product itself, and no trial has tested the fragment. KPV, a tripeptide from the end of α-MSH, calms inflammation in mouse colitis and has no randomized human trial.

points.en: BPC-157: rodents and case series
TB-500: a fragment, never trialled
KPV: mouse colitis only

body.en: A synthetic 15-residue peptide first described in 1993. Decades of rodent studies, most from one Zagreb group; in people, uncontrolled case series.
Sold as 'thymosin', but anti-doping chemists who analysed the product found a fragment — residues 17 to 23 — not the 43-residue parent. Ask what a patient actually bought.
The last three residues of α-MSH. Anti-inflammatory in mouse colitis models; no randomized human trials for any indication.

audioScript.en: Lesson three moves from the cosmetic shelf to the peptides patients buy online and inject. BPC-157 is a fifteen-residue peptide first described in 1993. Its evidence is a large rodent literature, most of it from one research group, and uncontrolled human case series. TB-500 is sold as thymosin, but when anti-doping chemists analysed the product they found a seven-residue fragment, residues seventeen to twenty-three of thymosin beta-four. That fragment has never been tested in a trial. KPV is the last three amino acids of alpha-MSH; it calms inflammation in mouse colitis models, and there is no randomized human trial of it for anything. All three have plausible mechanisms, and none has a controlled human trial.

body.en: As of September 2026 no randomized efficacy trial of BPC-157 in people has been published in full. FDA's July 2026 briefing found one randomized, placebo-controlled trial reported only as a 2005 meeting abstract: 53 people with ulcerative colitis, two weeks of treatment, and no significant difference from placebo. ClinicalTrials.gov adds a 2015 phase 1 safety study that never posted results, a completed 2025 single-arm product study with no results posted, and a randomized phase 1 trial after rotator-cuff surgery due to start in 2027.

label.en: randomized efficacy trials of BPC-157 in people published in full (September 2026)

detail.en: One 2005 ulcerative-colitis trial exists only as a meeting abstract (no significant difference from placebo) · registered: phase 1 safety study (2015, no results) · single-arm product study (2025, no results) · randomized phase 1 after rotator-cuff repair (starts 2027)

means.en: Whether BPC-157 helps people heal is unknown. The only randomized human result is an abstract that showed no significant benefit; the enthusiasm rests on rodents and uncontrolled case series.

doesNot.en: It does not show BPC-157 is ineffective or unsafe. Absence of trials is absence of evidence, and this figure will change when the registered trials report.

body.en: LL-37, the skin's own cathelicidin, is the one repair peptide with two randomized trials in hard-to-heal venous leg ulcers. Read them in order.

note.en: Multicentre phase IIb, placebo-controlled; only a post hoc subgroup signal
Sponsorship does not make a trial wrong; it is one more reason to wait for replication
A small positive trial followed by an adequately powered negative one

callout.en: A small positive trial is a hypothesis. LL-37 is what happens when someone tests it.

title.en: Where does it stand in the US?

body.en: Three US categories, dated to the FDA's category list of 14 May 2026 and the advisory-committee meeting of 23–24 July 2026. The committee's votes are advice; FDA must still act through rulemaking before anything joins the bulks list. FDA has sent warning letters naming GHK-Cu and BPC-157 on exactly this basis.

blocks.sourceNote: FDA 503A categories (14 May 2026) · 91 FR 20465 · PCAC 23–24 Jul 2026 · FDA warning letter 2020

note.en: No efficacy approval before sale; supplements may not claim to treat disease
FDA does not intend to act against compounders who meet its conditions while it evaluates
Compounded products do not qualify; an advisory-committee review is not approval

callout.en: Review is not approval. Check the live list before any conversation about compounding.

prompt.en: One product at a time: which US category is it in today?

why.en: A cosmetic ingredient, not a drug.
A dietary supplement: no disease claims, no efficacy approval.
Non-injectable GHK-Cu is in 503A Category 1 (FDA list of 14 May 2026), pending an advisory-committee consultation before the end of February 2027.
The Category 1 entry excludes injectable routes.
Reviewed by the advisory committee in July 2026; not on the bulks list unless and until FDA acts by rulemaking.
Same position as BPC-157 after the July 2026 review.

done.en: Six placed. Only one compounded peptide has Category 1 standing, and only for non-injectable use.

title.en: New dark patches, three months into 'GLOW'.

body.en: A 46-year-old patient has been injecting a research-use-only 'GLOW' blend bought online for three months. She reports smoother skin and asks about continuing. You notice new, patchy darkening on her face and forearms. This is a fictional case built from the lesson's evidence; there is one right first move.

blocks.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 15 · Pocket Guide · Vanhee 2020 · Ashraf 2024

setup.en: A 46-year-old patient has been injecting a research-use-only 'GLOW' blend bought online for three months. She reports smoother skin and asks about continuing. You notice new, patchy darkening on her face and forearms.

notice.en: GLOW is GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500: no controlled human trials of the blend
Research-use-only products are made outside GMP
The Hormonaly endocrinology guide treats new pigmentation on research-use-only peptides as a red flag

label.en: Reassure her: copper peptides can darken skin while collagen remodels. Review in three months.

why.en: There is no evidence for that explanation, and the guide reads new pigmentation on these products as a warning sign.

label.en: Advise stopping the product, record exactly what she bought, from where and the batch, and route the pigment change for clinical assessment.

why.en: Right. Stop the exposure, capture the evidence, and get the skin change assessed. Contamination with heavy metals is reported for this market but not documented; the change needs assessment either way.

label.en: Switch her to a compounded version of the same blend from a US pharmacy.

why.en: BPC-157, TB-500 and injectable GHK-Cu are not on the bulks list; a 'pharmacy version' does not solve the problem.

followUp.en: Then document the conversation: what she used, what you advised, and who assesses the pigmentation next.

interaction.source: authored:2026-09-24 from Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 15 RUO cautions + claim c-m04-16

prescriber.en: You assess the pigmentation or refer to dermatology, consider whether investigation is needed, and document the investigational product and your advice.

clinical-staff.en: You record the product, source and batch, photograph with consent if your setting allows, and escalate to the prescriber the same day.

advisor.en: You advise her to stop, keep the vial and packaging, and see a prescriber promptly; you do not suggest an alternative supplier.

audioScript.en: A fictional case, built from this lesson's evidence. A forty-six-year-old patient has been injecting a research-use-only blend sold as GLOW for three months: GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500 in one vial. She likes her skin and asks about carrying on. You notice new, patchy darkening on her face and forearms. The blend has no controlled human trials, it is made outside good manufacturing practice, and the Hormonaly guide treats new pigmentation on these products as a red flag. Impurity and mislabelling are documented for similar online products; heavy-metal contamination is reported for this market and has not been documented. Decide what you do first.

points.en: GLOW = GHK-Cu, BPC-157 and TB-500; no controlled human trials
Research-use-only products are made outside GMP
New pigmentation on these products is a red flag

body.en: A marketing name for three peptides in one vial, sold as research-use-only powder. No controlled trial has tested the blend.
New, patchy darkening on sun-exposed and covered skin, three months in. The Hormonaly endocrinology guide reads new pigmentation on research-use-only peptides as a warning sign.
Impurity and mislabelling are documented for adjacent products. Heavy-metal contamination is reported for this market but not documented; the skin change needs assessment either way.

why.en: The committee advises; nothing changes until FDA adds a substance to the bulks list by rulemaking.

text.en: Nothing yet: the committee advises, FDA must still act by rulemaking, and until then compounded products do not qualify for the 503A exemptions.

why.en: Correct. Review is not approval.

text.en: Only the injectable forms are restricted now.

why.en: None of the three is on the bulks list in any form; the injectable-only exception applies to GHK-Cu's Category 1 entry, not to these.

feedback.en: Check the live list. A pending review is not a licence to prescribe.

prompt.en: Closing Module 4: which statement keeps the four registers apart?

text.en: GHK-Cu has a strong mechanism, so its evidence grade is high.

why.en: That blends mechanism into human evidence. The mechanism is plausible; the human evidence is small (C).

text.en: Topical GHK-Cu: plausible copper-enzyme mechanism; small-trial human evidence (C); non-injectable Category 1 under FDA evaluation; whether it reaches the dermis in useful amounts is open.

why.en: Correct. Four separate answers, each with its own source.

text.en: Category 1 means FDA has approved GHK-Cu for skin.

why.en: Category 1 means 'still under evaluation' — an enforcement posture, not an approval.

feedback.en: Mechanism, human evidence, regulatory status, open question: four answers, never one sentence.

prompt.en: Which statement about topical GHK-Cu keeps its evidence and its regulatory status apart correctly?

text.en: It is GRADE C on small trials, and in the US its non-injectable form sits in 503A Category 1, which means under evaluation.

why.en: Correct. Two separate answers: small-trial human evidence, and an enforcement posture that is not an approval.

text.en: Its Category 1 listing shows FDA has found it effective for skin.

why.en: Category 1 means FDA is still evaluating; it says nothing about efficacy.

text.en: Its copper-enzyme mechanism makes its evidence grade A.

why.en: A plausible mechanism is not human evidence; the trials are small (C).

rationale.en: Mechanism, human evidence and regulatory status are separate registers; GHK-Cu scores differently on each.

prompt.en: Oral collagen trials pooled together look positive. What did splitting them by funding and quality show?

text.en: The benefit held in every subgroup.

why.en: It did not: independent and high-quality trials showed no effect.

text.en: The benefit appeared only in pharmaceutical-funded and lower-quality trials.

why.en: Correct — Myung and Park, 2025, 23 RCTs.
No harm signal was reported; the finding is about absence of benefit.

rationale.en: Funding and study quality can explain a pooled effect; ask who ran the trial before what it showed.

answer.en: Topical GHK-Cu has a plausible copper-enzyme mechanism and small-trial human support (GRADE C); injected GHK-Cu has no randomized trials and commonly irritates. In the US, as of FDA's 14 May 2026 list, non-injectable GHK-Cu is in 503A Category 1 (under evaluation, not approved); the injectable route is excluded. This course gives no doses or sourcing advice — for an individual patient, that is the prescriber's decision.

BPC-157's evidence is rodent studies from one group plus uncontrolled case series; no randomized efficacy trial in people has been published in full (September 2026); the one randomized trial FDA found, in ulcerative colitis, exists only as a 2005 meeting abstract and showed no significant difference from placebo. TB-500 is a seven-residue fragment of thymosin beta-4 that has never been trialled; KPV has only mouse data. GLOW and KLOW are marketing names for untested blends. FDA's advisory committee reviewed BPC-157, KPV and TB-500 in July 2026 — advice only; they are not on the 503A bulks list. New pigmentation while using research-use-only peptides is a red flag: stop, record the product and source, and get it assessed.
